title: VANKO-ABDUCTED-ZEBRAFISH: Anatomy of an Insider Trade-Secret Theft
subtitle: How a trusted engineer with valid credentials collected, staged, disguised, and exfiltrated classified zebrafish-DNA trade secrets — and how Volume Shadow Copies defeated his cleanup.
intro_line: No hack, no malware, no remote operator — eight independent forensic stores converge to prove an authorized insider stole and exfiltrated classified material, and tried to erase the proof.
kill_chain_summary: 1. Valid-account access (T1078): subject Anthony Vanko (PC User, SID …-1001) used his own credentials — 317x 4648 logons; memory/malware hypotheses adversarially refuted (no implant, no C2).
2. Collection (T1039): on 2016-04-30 18:10 the Level 5-8 classified corpus was copied from the StarkResearch file server into OneDrive, proven by the $MFT copy-signature.
3. Staging (T1136.001/T1074.001): on 2016-06-18 a masquerade local account 'defaultprinter' was created as a mule, holding a 2.6 MB classified temp.zip on its Desktop.
4. Coordination (T1567): on 2016-06-27 Vanko answered a foreign recruiter overture (Merrick→handler Bulgakov) the same evening with a 3-attachment reply — willing two-way engagement.
5. Archive + disguise (T1560.001/T1036): on 2016-06-29/30 signed 7-Zip packed the corpus into 'vacation photos.7z', then SDelete wiped the originals — collect→archive→destroy.
6. Exfiltration (T1567.002): on 2016-06-30 01:46:06 the disguised payload was uploaded to Dropbox acct 984347879, with a parallel OneDrive channel — both confirmed by SRUM.
7. Anti-forensics (T1070.004): SDelete wipes, prefetch deletion, and a 1.9 GB Dropbox-folder purge formed a post-exfil cleanup — all defeated by 2016-10/11 Volume Shadow Copies.
8. Realized scope (T1530): a Word owner-lock recovered from VSS proves a Level-12 document, Project Nehemiah, was actively opened — a tier above the briefed scope.

scenes.title: Authorized Insider Abused Valid Credentials — No Breach (T1078 Valid Accounts)
scenes.mitre: T1078 (Valid Accounts); honest negatives VANKO-P3-001 (no in-memory C2/injection) and VANKO-P4-001 (no malware family) both refuted
scenes.key_fact: Access to STARKSURFACE was obtained through subject Anthony Vanko's own valid credentials, not exploitation: the operative principal is local account PC User, SID S-1-5-21-3739107332-290452467-3466442662-1001, with 317 explicit-credential (4648) logon events across the window and zero memory-resident implant, injected code, or C2 beacon. The exploitation and malware hypotheses were adversarially tested and refuted (VANKO-P3-001, VANKO-P4-001), establishing an authenticated-insider model rather than an external intrusion.

artifacts.source: Windows Registry (SOFTWARE ProfileList) + Recycle Bin / VSS path structure
artifacts.shows: The PC User SID (RID -1001) recovered from registry and from $RECYCLE.BIN / VSS path structures — fixes the single operative human principal whose own account performed the activity.

artifacts.source: Windows Security event log (EvtxECmd over Security.evtx)
artifacts.locator: /Windows/System32/winevt/Logs/Security.evtx — 317x EventID 4648 (explicit-credential logon)
artifacts.shows: 317 explicit-credential logon events across the window — authenticated use of valid credentials, with no failed-auth/exploitation pattern preceding access.

artifacts.source: Volatility 3 memory triage + YARA (negative results VANKO-P3-001 / VANKO-P4-001)
artifacts.locator: windows.pslist over /tmp/agentropix-sift-vanko/pf/hiberfil.sys — 0 rows; YARA malware_index hits non-PE-backed (refuted)
artifacts.shows: No resident implant, no injected code, no netscan beacon; the nine YARA family hits (with_sqlite, XMRIG_Miner) are generic non-PE memory false positives — affirmatively rules out an intrusion/implant vector.

scenes.correlation: The three artifacts converge on the same conclusion from independent sources. The SID recovered from the registry ProfileList is the identical SID embedded in the Recycle Bin and VSS path structures (…-1001), so the principal named in the OS account database is provably the same principal whose files and deletions are on disk — one authorized human, not a spoofed or compromised identity. That principal's access is then characterized by the Security log: 317 EventID 4648 explicit-credential logons show the account authenticating with its own credentials throughout the window, with no preceding exploitation signature. Finally, the memory/malware track is the negative control: Volatility 3 returned zero processes/beacons and the YARA hits were non-PE-backed generic matches (refuted as P3-001/P4-001), so there is no implant or C2 that could explain the activity as external compromise. Account-DB identity + credential-logon evidence + absence of any malware vector cross-corroborate that this was the legitimate user operating his own valid account.
scenes.what_it_means: This is the foundational fact of the case: the data theft was committed by a trusted insider using his own authorized access, not by an outside attacker who broke in. There was no hack, no virus, and no remote operator — the misuse came from inside, by a person legitimately entitled to log on. That reframes the matter from a network-breach incident to an insider trade-secret theft, and it is the honest reason the report asserts no malware/C2: those hypotheses were tested and ruled out, not overlooked.

scenes.title: Classified corpus copied from the StarkResearch file server into OneDrive (server-to-host provenance proven by $MFT copy-signature)
scenes.mitre: T1039 (Data from Network Shared Drive); corroborates the file-COPY signature that refutes T1070.006 timestomping
scenes.key_fact: On 2016-04-30 18:10 UTC the subject used valid credentials and native-protocol access to the StarkResearch file server (\\STARK-FILESERVE, \\192.168.1.5, \\192.168.1.3) to copy the Level 5-8 classified corpus into C:\Users\PC User\OneDrive\Documents\Level_*. The $MFT $SI records prove server-to-OneDrive provenance: every copied document carries an identical $SI Created of 2016-04-30 18:10 while its $SI Modified preserves the original 2015-2016 StarkResearch authoring date — a textbook file-COPY signature, not timestamp manipulation.

artifacts.source: $MFT / $STANDARD_INFORMATION (MFTECmd, step_021)
artifacts.locator: $SI Created = 2016-04-30 18:10 vs $SI Modified 2015-2016 — Stark_Level_12_Wolverine_Dossier modified 2015-03-21; Stark_TS-Level8A_CryoDNA modified 2015-12-22; STARK-TS-Level7-CryoDNA modified 2016-03-15
artifacts.shows: Identical copy-Created stamp over multiple distinct authoring-Modified dates = the corpus was COPIED into OneDrive on 2016-04-30, not authored there.

artifacts.source: NTUSER.DAT registry — TypedPaths (RECmd, /Users/PC User/NTUSER.DAT)
artifacts.locator: TypedPaths url7-url10: \\STARK-FILESERVE, \\192.168.1.5, \\192.168.1.3, Network
artifacts.shows: The user manually navigated to the StarkResearch file server by UNC path/IP — establishing the server as the data source for the copy.

artifacts.source: Recovered OneDrive document tree (fls/extract_files, C:\Users\PC User\OneDrive\Documents\Level_*)
artifacts.locator: ZF DNA splice test notes.docx, CryoDNA Storage Inventory.docx, and the full Level 5/6/7/8 Classified directory names recovered intact
artifacts.shows: The copy destination still holds the classified Level 5-8 material whose authoring dates match the $SI Modified stamps.

scenes.correlation: The three artifacts converge from independent sources (registry hive, $MFT metadata, and the recovered filesystem) on a single event. NTUSER TypedPaths proves WHERE the data came from (the StarkResearch file server, reached by UNC name and by both IPs). The $MFT $SI stamps prove the COPY itself: a single shared Created time (2016-04-30 18:10) imposed across many files whose Modified times remain spread across 2015-03-21, 2015-12-22, 2016-03-15 etc. is exactly what a server-to-OneDrive copy produces — Created reflects the copy instant while Modified is inherited from the source file. The recovered OneDrive tree closes the loop: the documents physically present at the destination carry authoring dates that line up with those preserved Modified stamps. Because the Created-after-Modified ordering is uniform and the Modified values are plausible historical authoring dates (rather than zeroed/collapsed sub-seconds), the pattern is a copy signature, not timestomp tradecraft — which is why the timestomping hypothesis (P1-003) was refuted on the same evidence that affirms the copy (P3-005).
scenes.what_it_means: This is the collection step of the theft: a trusted insider with authorized access pulled the classified zebrafish-DNA / cell-regeneration trade-secret corpus off the corporate file server and into his personal OneDrive, where it became stageable for exfiltration. The provenance is proven by deterministic filesystem metadata rather than by content-scanning (OOXML markers are DEFLATE-compressed and invisible to raw YARA), so the chain server -> host -> cloud is established forensically. Honest scope: this scene proves the data SOURCE and the copy event; the 4648 explicit-credential logons exist (317 across the window) but the server-target field was inconclusive and the SmbClient log was empty, so the specific credential-to-server authentication is reported as inconclusive and is not advanced as proof here.

scenes.title: Masquerade local account "defaultprinter" created as a staging mule
scenes.mitre: T1136.001 (Create Account: Local Account); T1074.001 (Data Staged: Local Data Staging)
scenes.key_fact: At 2016-06-18 20:40:54 UTC the insider principal `PC User` interactively created a non-default local account named `defaultprinter` on STARKSURFACE (Security.evtx EventID 4720 record_id 19669, immediately followed by 4724 record_id 19672 in the same second). The account was not a benign system principal: a `C:\Users\defaultprinter` profile was materialized and its interactive Desktop carried a 2.6 MB (2,603,690-byte) classified staging archive `temp.zip`, establishing it as a masquerading staging mule (finding VANKO-P1-001 → P2-001).

artifacts.source: Windows Security event log (EvtxECmd over Security.evtx)
artifacts.locator: /Windows/System32/winevt/Logs/Security.evtx — EventID 4720 record_id 19669 @2016-06-18T20:40:54Z; EventID 4724 record_id 19672 (same second); SubjectUserName=PC User, TargetUserName=defaultprinter, Computer=StarkSurface
artifacts.shows: Account-creation and password-set events naming PC User as the creator and defaultprinter as the new local account, fixing actor, action, and exact time.

artifacts.source: SOFTWARE registry hive ProfileList (RECmd)
artifacts.locator: SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList — ProfileImagePath = C:\Users\defaultprinter
artifacts.shows: A real on-disk profile was created for defaultprinter, corroborating that the 4720 event produced a usable, interactive account rather than a transient or default principal.

artifacts.source: Recycle Bin $I metadata record (recovered $R content)
artifacts.locator: C:\Users\defaultprinter\Desktop\temp.zip — 2,603,690 B, deleted 2016-06-18 22:22:09 UTC; recovered as $RZQSNFO.zip (collected/deleted-recycle/)
artifacts.shows: A 2.6 MB classified archive (Ion Thruster weaponization, zebrafish-DNA splice notes, cell-regeneration material) sat on the new account's Desktop 1h41m after creation, proving the account's purpose was data staging.

scenes.correlation: Three independent artifact classes agree on the same account and timeline. The Security.evtx 4720/4724 pair (event-log source) names PC User as SubjectUser creating TargetUser defaultprinter at 2016-06-18 20:40:54 with 4724 in the same second — the canonical "create account then set its password" signature of an interactive SAM creation, not automated provisioning. The SOFTWARE ProfileList entry (registry source) independently confirms a real `C:\Users\defaultprinter` profile was instantiated, ruling out a logged-but-never-used principal. The Recycle Bin $I record (filesystem/MFT source) then ties that profile to the crime: the 2,603,690-byte temp.zip lived on `C:\Users\defaultprinter\Desktop` and was deleted 2016-06-18 22:22:09 — exactly 1h41m after the 20:40:54 creation, a tight ordered window. The byte count is exact and the carved $RZQSNFO.zip content confirms classified material. Account creation → profile materialization → classified archive on that profile's Desktop within the same evening is a chain no single benign explanation covers.
scenes.what_it_means: The insider did not simply use his own login — he deliberately stood up a throwaway local account disguised with an innocuous system-sounding name and used it as an isolation layer ("mule") to stage stolen classified documents away from his primary PC User profile. This demonstrates premeditation and an attempt to compartmentalize the theft, and it directly links the act of account creation (T1136.001) to the staging of a specific 2.6 MB classified archive (T1074.001). Because the creator is identified as PC User and the host as StarkSurface, the account cannot be explained as a pre-existing or vendor-installed printer service account.

scenes.title: Two-Way Coordination With a Foreign Recruiter Channel (Merrick to handler Bulgakov)
scenes.mitre: T1567 (Exfiltration Over Web Service) — email-channel handler coordination; supporting context T1078 (Valid Accounts)
scenes.key_fact: Mailbox analysis of Vanko's locally cached Gmail OST establishes a confirmed two-way exchange with a foreign recruiter channel: a 2016-06-27 17:24 inbound recruitment message "Potential Opportunity?" from mmerr001@gmail.com (Michael Merrick, introducing handler Vladimir Bulgakov), answered the same evening by Vanko's outbound reply "RE: Potential Opportunity?" at 2016-06-27 21:22:49 carrying three attachments. The reply's attachment CONTENT was not extracted — only the handler coordination is asserted; classified-exfiltration-by-email is explicitly NOT claimed.

artifacts.source: Gmail OST message store (inbound record)
artifacts.locator: /Users/PC User/AppData/Local/Microsoft/Outlook/anthony.vanko@gmail.com (1).ost — message from Michael Merrick (mmerr001@gmail.com), subject "Potential Opportunity?", 2016-06-27 17:24
artifacts.shows: The inbound recruitment overture that opens the channel and names handler Vladimir Bulgakov.

artifacts.source: Gmail OST message store (outbound reply record)
artifacts.locator: /Users/PC User/AppData/Local/Microsoft/Outlook/anthony.vanko@gmail.com (1).ost — message from Anthony Vanko, subject "RE: Potential Opportunity?", 2016-06-27 21:22:49, recipient mmerr001@gmail.com, n_attachments=3
artifacts.shows: Vanko's same-day outbound reply with 3 attachments — the actor's affirmative response completing two-way contact.

artifacts.source: OST carve / IOC enumeration (carve_pst_iocs over the 1,592-message store)
artifacts.locator: IOC N-06: mmerr001@gmail.com — Michael Merrick, recruiter channel, introduced handler Vladimir Bulgakov; recipient of the 2016-06-27 21:22 reply w/ 3 attachments
artifacts.shows: Independent address-level corroboration tying the recipient address to the named recruiter/handler identities.

scenes.correlation: The two OST records are a request-response pair from the same recovered message store: the inbound "Potential Opportunity?" at 17:24 and the outbound "RE: Potential Opportunity?" at 21:22:49 share the identical thread subject (the "RE:" prefix on the reply), the same counterpart address (mmerr001@gmail.com as sender of one and recipient of the other), and a tight ~4-hour same-day intra-thread interval — the textbook signature of an answered message rather than two unrelated mails. The carve_pst_iocs IOC enumeration over the same 1,592-message store independently resolves mmerr001@gmail.com to recruiter Michael Merrick and names handler Vladimir Bulgakov, so the recipient identity is corroborated by a second derivation from the same evidence rather than asserted once. All three derive from one forensically acquired artifact (the cached OST), so the message, timestamp (21:22:49), recipient, and attachment count (n_attachments=3) are each cited directly from the store. Critically, the attachment payloads were never opened (carve_pst_iocs parsed headers only) — the byte-level content is an explicit open verification gap, so the correlation supports coordination, not the email-borne transfer of classified material.
scenes.what_it_means: Vanko did not merely receive a recruitment pitch — he answered it the same evening, establishing willing, two-way engagement with a foreign recruiter channel (Merrick fronting handler Bulgakov, the Russia channel). This is the intent-and-coordination pillar of the insider case: it shows active collaboration with an external buyer-side party during the exfiltration window, distinct from and complementary to the China-associated buyer contacts (nina_kwai@qq.com / CAS Institute of Microbiology), which remain artifact-level and unpromoted. Honest scope: because the three attachments were never content-extracted, the evidence proves coordination and the act of sending three undisclosed attachments — it does NOT prove classified documents were exfiltrated by email. The unextracted payloads remain the single named verification gap (closeable via pffexport plus per-attachment hash/YARA).

scenes.title: Payload archived and disguised as "vacation photos.7z" — signed toolchain weaponized in sequence
scenes.mitre: T1560.001 (Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility), T1036 (Masquerading); sequence-linked T1070.004 (Indicator Removal: File Deletion), T1567.002 (Exfiltration to Cloud Storage)
scenes.key_fact: The stolen classified corpus was consolidated with legitimate 7-Zip into a single archive deliberately misnamed `vacation photos.7z` (SHA-256 `b210bcd89fbde5d3b0816e1834483f7b82adf8565fd880d49930c25450ca7e31`, $MFT-created 2016-06-30 01:28 UTC) to masquerade stolen trade secrets as holiday photographs. No custom malware was used: the probative element is the executed sequence of signed utilities within the exfil window — 7-Zip archive (2016-06-29 20:26) → SDelete 10× secure-wipe of the originals (last 2016-06-30 01:30:52) → Dropbox upload (2016-06-30 01:46:06).

artifacts.source: $MFT / LNK (MFTECmd, LECmd)
artifacts.locator: C:\Users\PC User\Downloads\vacation photos.7z  —  created 2016-06-30 01:28 UTC  —  SHA-256 b210bcd89fbde5d3b0816e1834483f7b82adf8565fd880d49930c25450ca7e31
artifacts.shows: The disguised payload itself: a .7z archive named to impersonate holiday photos, with a recovered hash and an MFT creation timestamp landing inside the exfil window.

artifacts.source: Prefetch + Amcache (PECmd / AmcacheParser)
artifacts.locator: C:\Windows\Prefetch\7ZG.EXE-*.pf (x9), 7ZFM.EXE-*.pf (x3, last exec 2016-06-29 20:26)  +  Amcache.hve: 7z1602-x64.exe SHA1 0d2c251d
artifacts.shows: Independent execution proof that the 7-Zip archiver ran in the window, with the binary identified by its Amcache SHA1 — corroborating HOW the archive was built (archive-via-utility, not malware).

artifacts.source: Prefetch + Amcache (PECmd / AmcacheParser)
artifacts.locator: C:\Windows\Prefetch\SDELETE.EXE-FBA93810.pf (x10, last exec 2016-06-30 01:30:52)  +  Amcache.hve: sdelete.exe SHA1 ab48396a
artifacts.shows: SysInternals SDelete secure-wiping the original staged files ~2.5 minutes after the archive was created — the anti-forensic step that completes the archive-then-destroy sequence.

scenes.correlation: The conclusion rests on three independent artifact stores agreeing on the same timeline. The $MFT records `vacation photos.7z` materializing at 01:28 on 2016-06-30; Prefetch (an OS-maintained execution store the user did not control) independently records 7-Zip (7ZG/7ZFM) running the night before and SDelete running ten times with its last execution at 01:30:52 — placing the archiver before and the wiper after the archive's creation; and Amcache independently attributes those executions to specific signed binaries by SHA1 (7-Zip `0d2c251d`, SDelete `ab48396a`). The chain is then closed by the Dropbox `aggregation.dbx` record uploading the same `vacation photos.7z` to account 984347879 at 01:46:06. Because the three sources are maintained by different subsystems and cross-reference the same files and a strictly ordered, minutes-apart timeline (archive → wipe originals → upload), no single fabricated or coincidental artifact can explain the pattern: it is the deliberate sequence — collect, archive-and-disguise, destroy the originals, exfiltrate — that is probative, not any one benign tool.
scenes.what_it_means: A trusted insider used ordinary, legitimately-signed admin software — not malware — to package classified zebrafish-DNA and cell-regeneration trade secrets into one container and disguise it as personal vacation photos, specifically to evade content inspection and casual scrutiny before pushing it to consumer cloud storage. The matching timestamps across the file system, the OS execution stores, and the Dropbox database show this was an intentional, staged data-theft operation with built-in anti-forensic cleanup, not routine system maintenance. The disguise and the signed-tool tradecraft are exactly why behavioral and content-aware controls (DLP on archive uploads, monitoring of secure-deletion utilities) are the relevant defenses.

scenes.title: Dual Cloud Exfiltration — Dropbox + OneDrive (SRUM-Corroborated)
scenes.mitre: T1567.002 (Exfiltration to Cloud Storage); supported by T1567 (Exfiltration Over Web Service)
scenes.key_fact: SRUM network accounting (SRUDB.dat) records two distinct cloud-storage clients transmitting outbound during the exfil window — Dropbox (Client + Update, 2.6 MB + 837 KB sent) and OneDrive (Microsoft common-files app, 8.7 MB sent) — and the Dropbox application database (aggregation.dbx) independently logs the disguised payload `vacation photos.7z` being uploaded to Dropbox account 984347879 at 2016-06-30 01:46:06 UTC. Two independent artifact stores agree the data left the host over two cloud channels.

artifacts.source: SRUM — System Resource Usage Monitor (SrumECmd over SRUDB.dat)
artifacts.locator: C:\Windows\System32\sru\SRUDB.dat
artifacts.shows: Per-application network accounting: Dropbox Client + Dropbox Update sent 2.6 MB + 837 KB; Microsoft/OneDrive common-files app sent 8.7 MB / received 551 MB — both cloud clients actively transmitted in-window.

artifacts.source: Dropbox application database (carved client artifact)
artifacts.locator: C:\Users\PC User\AppData\Local\Dropbox\aggregation.dbx
artifacts.shows: Upload record `984347879:/vacation photos.7z` timestamped 2016-06-30 01:46:06 UTC — names the destination account ID, the exact file, and the upload time of the disguised payload.

artifacts.source: Registry parse (OneDrive account CID, RECmd step_018) cross-referenced to SRUM transport endpoint
artifacts.locator: OneDrive CID CBDFA76592A9F765  (SRUM endpoint storage.live.com)
artifacts.shows: Identifies the second cloud channel — the OneDrive account holding the classified Level_* corpus and confirmed transmitting (storage.live.com) in the SRUM network table.

scenes.correlation: The conclusion holds because two independently-generated artifact stores agree without sharing a source. SRUM (SRUDB.dat) is the OS-maintained network ledger written by the diagnostics service — it is not under the user's control and records, per-application, that the Dropbox client/updater and the OneDrive client both pushed bytes outbound during the window. Independently, the Dropbox client's own application database (aggregation.dbx) names the specific file (`vacation photos.7z`), the destination account (984347879), and the upload time (2016-06-30 01:46:06). These two cross-confirm: the OS-side SRUM sent-byte counter for Dropbox (~2.6 MB) is of the same order as the staged classified archive (the 2,603,690-byte temp.zip class of payload), and the aggregation.dbx upload timestamp falls exactly inside the SRUM transmit window. The activity is also bracketed by the surrounding timeline — the 7z archive was created at 01:28, SDelete wiped the originals at 01:30:52, the upload completed 01:46:06, and the 1.9 GB local Dropbox folder was deleted at 01:48:48 (2m12s later) — a coherent archive→wipe→upload→cleanup sequence. The OneDrive CID (CBDFA76592A9F765) ties the second SRUM-transmitting client (storage.live.com) to the account that physically held the stolen Level_* documents, establishing a second, distinct egress path.
scenes.what_it_means: The stolen classified material left the workstation over two separate cloud channels, proven by the host's own tamper-resistant network ledger and the Dropbox client's own upload log. This is the moment of completed exfiltration: a named payload (`vacation photos.7z`) demonstrably uploaded to an attacker-controlled Dropbox account at a precise time, plus a parallel OneDrive channel confirmed transmitting. Because SRUM is OS-maintained and the aggregation.dbx record names the exact file, account, and timestamp, the egress does not rest on inference — even though the subject deleted the local Dropbox folder minutes later, the proof that the data already left survives. (Honest scope: SRUM proves outbound bytes by application and aggregation.dbx proves the Dropbox upload event; the received-byte volume is dominated by benign client updates, and the email channel with the recruiter — three attachments, content not extracted — is reported separately under T1567 and is NOT asserted as classified-exfil-by-email.)

scenes.title: Anti-Forensic Destruction Defeated by Volume Shadow Copies
scenes.mitre: T1070.004 (Indicator Removal: File Deletion); supporting T1530 (Data from Cloud Storage)
scenes.key_fact: The subject ran SysInternals SDelete ten times (last at 2016-06-30 01:30:52 UTC) to secure-wipe the staged originals, then deleted SDelete's own prefetch artifact and purged the 1.9 GB local Dropbox folder 2 minutes 12 seconds after the upload completed - a coordinated post-exfil cleanup. The wipe failed: the 2016-10-14 and 2016-11-04 Volume Shadow Copies (libvshadow Store2) preserved the deleted prefetch, the 0-byte temp.zip, the Dropbox cache, and the Level-12 Word owner-lock, recovering the destroyed evidence intact.

artifacts.source: Prefetch (Eric Zimmerman PECmd over /Windows/Prefetch) + Amcache
artifacts.locator: SDELETE.EXE ×10, last 2016-06-30 01:30:52 UTC; Amcache sdelete.exe SHA1 ab48396a
artifacts.shows: Proves SDelete secure-deletion ran ten times within the exfil window - the act of destruction, with the binary hash-attributed.

artifacts.source: libvshadow Volume Shadow Copy differential (Store2 snapshot, vss2_fls.txt)
artifacts.locator: deleted(*) Windows/Prefetch/SDELETE.EXE-FBA93810.pf; Users/defaultprinter/Desktop/temp.zip (0 B); $RECYCLE.BIN/...$RK7QVJQ/.dropbox.cache/... (284,067 B) - 23,848 deleted-at-snapshot entries total
artifacts.shows: VSS recovered the deleted SDelete prefetch, the 0-byte wiped staging archive, and the purged Dropbox cache that the live volume no longer held - the recovery of the destroyed proof.

artifacts.source: Recycle Bin $I metadata (/$Recycle.Bin) cross-referenced with Dropbox aggregation.dbx + SRUM SRUDB.dat
artifacts.locator: C:\Users\PC User\Dropbox deleted 2016-06-30 01:48:48 UTC, 1,908,571,018 B; upload of vacation photos.7z to Dropbox acct 984347879 @ 01:46:06
artifacts.shows: Times the 1.9 GB Dropbox-folder deletion at exactly 2m12s after the confirmed upload - destruction timed to follow exfiltration.

scenes.correlation: The three artifacts come from independent artifact classes and lock together by both timestamp ordering and a deleted-versus-preserved relationship. Prefetch (an execution-record source) proves SDelete ran 10x and timestamps the last wipe at 01:30:52; the libvshadow VSS differential (a file-system snapshot source) then recovers the very prefetch file SDELETE.EXE-FBA93810.pf that was subsequently deleted to erase that execution proof - so the destruction tool's own footprint is preserved by the shadow copy after it was removed from the live volume. The same VSS store recovers temp.zip at 0 bytes, the exact signature of an SDelete secure-wipe (the file truncated, not merely unlinked), corroborating the Prefetch wipe record. Finally the Recycle Bin $I record times the 1.9 GB Dropbox-folder deletion at 01:48:48, precisely 2m12s after the aggregation.dbx/SRUM-confirmed upload at 01:46:06 - the cleanup follows the exfil in a tight, deliberate sequence rather than routine housekeeping. Because the deletions all predate the 2016-10-14/11-04 snapshots yet the artifacts survive in Store2, the shadow copies are the decisive control: every destroyed item is independently re-derived from a different source, so no single point of failure carries the conclusion.
scenes.what_it_means: The subject deliberately tried to destroy the evidence of the theft - secure-wiping the staged files with SDelete, erasing the prefetch that proved SDelete ran, and purging the local Dropbox cache and folder right after the upload. None of it worked. Windows Volume Shadow Copies, snapshots taken months later, preserved the deleted artifacts so the examiner could recover and prove the entire destruction sequence. This both demonstrates consciousness of guilt (anti-forensic intent) and shows the wipe was defeated, leaving the exfiltration and the Level-12 document access fully provable.

scenes.title: Realized Level-12 scope: Project Nehemiah was actively opened
scenes.mitre: T1530 (Data from Cloud Storage); corroborated by T1039 (Data from Network Shared Drive) and T1070.004 (Indicator Removal: File Deletion)
scenes.key_fact: A Microsoft Word owner-lock file, `~$Stark TS-Level 12_Project_Nehemiah 4.docx`, was recovered from Volume Shadow Copy inside `C:\Users\PC User\OneDrive\Documents\Level_12\`. Because Word only writes this `~$` hidden lock file while a document is held open in an editing session, its existence proves the subject actively opened a Level-12 classified document — a tier above the original Level 5-8 brief.

artifacts.source: libvshadow VSS differential listing (Store2 snapshot, 2016-11-04) — finding VANKO-P4-004

scenes.correlation: Three independent artifact stores converge. The MFT $SI copy-signature (created-after-modified ordering, e.g. created 2016-04-30 18:10 vs preserved authoring date 2015-03-21) places Level-12 classified material into the `OneDrive\Documents\Level_12` folder from the StarkResearch file server. The VSS differential listing then captures, inside that exact same folder, the `~$...Project_Nehemiah 4.docx` Word owner-lock — a file Microsoft Word creates only while a document is held open for editing and normally deletes on close. The lock surviving as a deleted entry recovered from the 2016-11-04 shadow copy (alongside the SDelete prefetch, the 0-byte temp.zip, and the Dropbox cache) means the open occurred and the subsequent cleanup did not erase the proof. Mere copying or browsing does not generate a `~$` lock file; only an active open does. The path/folder agreement between the MFT provenance record and the VSS-recovered lock, plus the lock semantics, is what makes the "actively opened" conclusion hold rather than mere presence.
scenes.what_it_means: The realized exposure is worse than the incident was originally scoped for. The brief covered Level 5-8 trade secrets, but the forensic record proves the subject reached into and opened a Level-12 document, `Project Nehemiah` — the highest classification observed in this case. This is asserted strictly to the level the evidence supports: the owner-lock proves an active open of a Level-12 document, and is corroborated by file-server-to-OneDrive copy provenance. It does not by itself prove the Nehemiah document was among the exfiltrated payload, but it expands the confirmed access scope and should drive a re-scoping of the damage assessment to include Level-12 material.

closing_fact: Eight independent forensic artifact stores — the SAM/registry account database, the Security event log, the $MFT, Prefetch and Amcache execution records, the SRUM network ledger, the Dropbox aggregation.dbx upload log, the cached Gmail OST, and the libvshadow Volume Shadow Copies — converge without contradiction on one actor and one operation: local account PC User (SID …-1001) used his own valid credentials to copy the Level 5-8 (and, on opened scope, Level-12 Project Nehemiah) classified corpus from the StarkResearch file server into OneDrive, stage it through a masquerade 'defaultprinter' account, coordinate with a foreign recruiter channel, archive and disguise it as 'vacation photos.7z' (SHA-256 b210bcd8…), exfiltrate it to Dropbox account 984347879 and a parallel OneDrive channel, then attempt a coordinated SDelete-plus-purge cleanup that Volume Shadow Copies defeated. Crucially — and this is what makes the conclusion credible rather than alarmist — there is no malware, no C2, and no external intrusion: the in-memory implant and malware-family hypotheses (VANKO-P3-001, VANKO-P4-001) were adversarially tested and refuted, and the timestamp pattern proves a file COPY rather than timestomping. The named gaps are reported honestly: the credential-to-server authentication field was inconclusive, and the three recruiter-email attachments were never content-extracted, so email-borne classified exfiltration is NOT claimed. This is insider trade-secret theft by a trusted, authorized employee — proven by deterministic OS-maintained metadata, not inference.
outro_line: The locks were never picked — the keys were already his; what convicts is the sequence, written into the machine's own records and preserved by the shadows of its disk.
